demographics: Worldwide, most adults are infected with HSV-1; HSV-2 prevalence rises after sexual debut
Genital herpes is more commonly diagnosed in women than men
Orolabial herpes affects all ages, including young children

risk_factors.text: Unprotected sexual contact with an infected partner
Multiple sexual partners or a new sexual partner
Close nonsexual contact with someone who has active oral lesions (e.g., kissing, sharing utensils)
Occupational exposure (healthcare workers, contact sports such as wrestling)

comorbidities: Prior history of genital or orolabial herpes
social_history: May have a partner with a history of cold sores or genital herpes
exposures: Direct skin-to-skin or mucosal contact with an infected person
Sexual contact with an infected partner
Kissing or sharing utensils with someone who has an active cold sore

chief_complaints.text: I have painful blisters on my genitals
I have a tingling or burning sore on my lip
I feel like I have the flu

hpi.onset: Primary infection: gradual over 1–2 days after an incubation period of about 2–12 days. Recurrent infection: abrupt, often preceded by tingling, itching or burning at the site for hours to a day.
hpi.duration: Lesions last 7–10 days in primary infection; recurrences are shorter, typically 3–7 days.
hpi.progression: Starts with localized tingling, burning or itching, followed by small grouped blisters that rupture and form painful ulcers, then crust and heal without scarring. Primary episodes are more severe and may be accompanied by systemic symptoms; recurrences are milder and shorter.
hpi.location: Orolabial: lips, mouth, face. Genital: vulva, vagina, cervix, penis, scrotum, buttocks, anus or thighs. Other sites: fingers (herpetic whitlow), eyes (keratoconjunctivitis), skin (eczema herpeticum).
hpi.radiation: Pain may radiate to the groin or legs with genital lesions; oral lesions may cause referred ear pain.
hpi.quality: Painful, burning, tingling, itchy; ulcers are tender to touch.
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; primary genital herpes can be very painful (7–10/10), while recurrences are usually mild to moderate.
hpi.timing: Continuous until healed; recurrences can be triggered by stress, illness, fever, sunlight, menstruation or trauma.
aggravating: Eating or drinking acidic foods (oral lesions)

associated_symptoms.text: Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the groin or neck

pertinent_negatives: No new medications or other trigger for the rash
No history of similar lesions before (for primary episode)
No visual changes or eye pain (unless ocular involvement)
No recent travel or tick exposure
No lesions elsewhere on the body

positives.text: Tingling or itching before the sores appear

negatives: Rash on the palms and soles

positives.text: Sores on the lips or inside the mouth

atypical.how_it_differs: Lesions are more extensive, persist longer, may become chronic and can disseminate to multiple sites; systemic symptoms are more prominent.
Primary oral infection (gingivostomatitis) is common in young children and presents with fever, irritability, refusal to eat, and multiple vesicles and ulcers in the mouth and on the lips.
Primary infection near delivery carries a high risk of neonatal transmission; recurrent lesions are usually milder but still require careful management.
May present with atypical orofacial pain or neuralgia without obvious vesicles (e.g., postherpetic neuralgia-like symptoms), and lesions may be less vesicular.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, may grimace when the affected area is touched or during urination
general.severe: Ill-appearing, visibly uncomfortable, reluctant to sit or walk due to genital pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, febrile, lethargic; consider disseminated disease or CNS involvement

findings.maneuver: Inspect the affected skin and mucosa in good light
findings.finding: Small grouped fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently touch any ruptured lesions
findings.finding: Shallow, tender ulcers with a red base after vesicles rupture

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, oral mucosa, tongue and gingiva
findings.finding: Vesicles or ulcers on the lips, gingiva, tongue or buccal mucosa; may be grouped

findings.maneuver: Inspect the vulva, vagina, penis, scrotum, perineum and perianal area
findings.finding: Vesicles or ulcers on the external genitalia, perineum or perianal skin

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal lymph node chains bilaterally
Palpate the cervical lymph node chains
findings.finding: Tender, enlarged cervical lymph nodes with orolabial disease

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to describe any sensation at the site before lesions appeared
findings.finding: Localized tingling, burning or itching preceding the eruption

findings.maneuver: Inspect the fingers and nail folds
findings.finding: Painful grouped vesicles on a finger or around a nail

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and cornea with a light; check for photophobia
findings.finding: Conjunctival injection, corneal dendritic lesions or photophobia suggesting keratitis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk, palms and soles
findings.finding: No target lesions, no rash on palms and soles
No honey-colored crusting typical of impetigo

findings.maneuver: Assess neck flexion and general neurologic status
findings.finding: No neck stiffness, confusion or focal neurologic deficit
No joint swelling, warmth or tenderness

labs.caveat: Mild leukocytosis may accompany a severe primary episode; a normal count does not exclude herpes.
Only if CNS involvement is suspected; a lymphocytic pleocytosis supports herpes encephalitis or meningitis.
Mildly low or normal; markedly low glucose points to bacterial or fungal meningitis.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected herpes encephalitis or first seizure

findings.text: Normal study early in the course

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without contrast

findings.text: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal and inferior frontal lobes
Usually normal; may show focal or diffuse opacities if pneumonia complicates disseminated disease

initial.why: Swab of a fresh vesicle or ulcer base is the preferred test to confirm herpes simplex
Type-specific serology identifies HSV-1 versus HSV-2 and prior infection
Standard testing with a new sexually transmitted infection
Syphilis is a common look-alike for genital ulcers
Assesses for leukocytosis in a severe primary episode
initial.only_if: systemic symptoms or severe primary episode

initial.why: Supports an inflammatory or severe primary episode
initial.only_if: systemic symptoms or severe primary episode

supporting.only_if: headache with fever, confusion, seizure or neck stiffness

supporting.why: Helps distinguish viral from bacterial meningitis

supporting.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
supporting.why: Temporal lobe changes support herpes encephalitis

not_indicated.why: Not recommended; poor specificity and cross-reactivity
Not needed for uncomplicated skin or genital lesions

not_indicated.only_if: disseminated disease or respiratory symptoms are suspected

decision_points: Swab a fresh vesicle or ulcer base for PCR; crusted or healing lesions lower the yield
Offer HIV and syphilis testing with any new genital ulcer
Consider herpes encephalitis and start empiric acyclovir when fever, headache, confusion or seizures accompany oral or genital lesions
In pregnancy near delivery, notify obstetrics because primary infection carries a high risk of neonatal transmission

differential.name: Syphilis
differential.why_considered: Painless or minimally painful genital ulcer; a classic look-alike for genital herpes
differential.trigger: Any genital ulcer, especially a single indurated painless one

history: Ulcer present for weeks and healing spontaneously
exam: Regional lymphadenopathy that is firm and nontender
labs: Darkfield or PCR positive for Treponema pallidum

differential.name: Chancroid
differential.why_considered: Painful genital ulcer with tender inguinal lymph nodes

history: Recent sexual contact in an endemic area
labs: Haemophilus ducreyi identified by culture or PCR

differential.name: Herpes zoster
differential.why_considered: Painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base

history: Does not recur in the same pattern

differential.name: Aphthous ulcers
differential.why_considered: Painful oral ulcers that can mimic intraoral herpes

history: No prodrome of tingling or vesicles
Associated with stress, trauma or inflammatory bowel disease
exam: Round ulcer with a yellow-gray base and red halo

differential.name: Impetigo
differential.why_considered: Crusted skin lesions around the mouth or face

exam: No grouped vesicles or prodromal tingling
labs: Gram stain or culture grows Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes

differential.name: Behçet disease
differential.why_considered: Recurrent painful oral and genital ulcers

history: Skin lesions such as erythema nodosum
labs: No specific test; diagnosis is clinical

differential.name: Erythema multiforme
differential.why_considered: Painful oral ulcers and skin lesions, often after herpes simplex infection

exam: Target lesions with three concentric zones
Oral ulcers but no grouped vesicles
labs: HSV PCR may be positive but skin biopsy shows interface dermatitis

differential.name: Herpes encephalitis
differential.why_considered: Fever, headache, confusion or seizures with oral or genital lesions
differential.trigger: Fever with headache, confusion, seizure or focal neurologic deficit in a patient with herpes lesions

imaging: Temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity on MRI

severity.mild: Recurrent orolabial or genital lesions: localized tingling or itching followed by a few grouped vesicles, no systemic symptoms, resolves in 3–7 days
severity.moderate: Primary orolabial or genital infection: multiple painful vesicles and ulcers, tender regional lymphadenopathy, low-grade fever, dysuria, resolves in 7–10 days
severity.severe: Extensive primary infection with severe pain, high fever, inability to eat or urinate, or lesions in multiple sites; may require hospitalization for hydration and pain control
severity.critical: Disseminated herpes simplex with visceral involvement, herpes encephalitis, or neonatal herpes; life-threatening and requires IV acyclovir

red_flags.finding: Fever with headache, confusion, seizure or focal neurologic deficit
red_flags.meaning: Possible herpes encephalitis; start empiric IV acyclovir and obtain CSF PCR and MRI

red_flags.finding: Disseminated vesicles with fever and malaise in an immunocompromised patient
red_flags.meaning: Disseminated herpes simplex; requires IV acyclovir and evaluation for visceral involvement

red_flags.finding: Neonate with vesicles, lethargy, poor feeding or seizures
red_flags.meaning: Neonatal herpes; emergency requiring IV acyclovir

red_flags.finding: Eye redness, pain, photophobia or blurred vision
red_flags.meaning: Herpes keratitis; urgent ophthalmology referral to prevent vision loss

red_flags.finding: Inability to urinate or severe pain preventing oral intake
red_flags.meaning: Urinary retention or dehydration; may need catheterization and IV fluids

special_populations.differences: Primary oral infection (gingivostomatitis) is common in young children and presents with fever, irritability, refusal to eat, and multiple vesicles and ulcers in the mouth and on the lips.
Neonatal herpes can present with vesicles, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures or sepsis-like illness; requires urgent IV acyclovir.
May present with atypical orofacial pain or neuralgia without obvious vesicles, and lesions may be less vesicular.
Primary infection near delivery carries a high risk of neonatal transmission; recurrent lesions are usually milder but still require careful management and obstetric involvement.
Lesions are more extensive, persist longer, may become chronic and can disseminate to multiple sites; systemic symptoms are more prominent and IV therapy is often needed.

key_questions.question: What did the sore look like when it first appeared, and how has it changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Grouped small fluid-filled blisters on a red base that rupture into shallow painful ulcers and then crust and heal

key_questions.question: Did you notice any tingling, itching or burning at the spot before the sores appeared?
key_questions.looking_for: A localized prodrome for hours to a day before the eruption, typical of herpes

key_questions.question: Where exactly are the sores?
key_questions.looking_for: Lips, mouth or face (orolabial) or vulva, vagina, penis, scrotum, buttocks, perineum or anus (genital)

key_questions.question: Have you had sores like this before, and if so how often do they come back?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes at the same site suggest reactivation of latent HSV

key_questions.question: How long do the sores last, and do they heal without scarring?
key_questions.looking_for: About 7–10 days for a primary episode, 3–7 days for recurrences, healing without scarring

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you urinate, or is it hard to urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria or urinary retention with genital lesions

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, headache, muscle aches or felt generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic symptoms are more common with a primary episode

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swollen or tender lumps in your groin or neck?
Are you sexually active, and do you use condoms? Have you had a new partner recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Sexual exposure risk for genital herpes and need for STI testing

key_questions.question: Does your partner have a history of cold sores or genital herpes?
key_questions.looking_for: A known infected partner as the source of exposure

key_questions.question: Have you ever been tested for HIV or other sexually transmitted infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior STI testing and any known HIV or immunosuppression

key_questions.question: Do you take any medicines that weaken the immune system, such as steroids or transplant medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, which predicts more extensive and prolonged disease

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant, and when was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, especially near delivery, because primary infection carries a high risk of neonatal transmission

key_questions.question: Do you have any redness, pain, tearing or sensitivity to light in your eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Ocular involvement suggesting herpes keratitis, which needs urgent ophthalmology referral

key_questions.question: Have you had a stiff neck, confusion, a seizure or weakness anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Possible herpes encephalitis or meningitis requiring urgent CSF testing and IV acyclovir

reasoning_points: Grouped small fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base that rupture into shallow painful ulcers and heal without scarring
A localized prodrome of tingling, burning or itching before the lesions appear
Recurrent episodes at the same site, consistent with reactivation of latent HSV
Primary episodes are more severe and longer, with fever, malaise and tender regional lymphadenopathy; recurrences are milder and shorter
Distribution fits orolabial or genital/perineal sites, matching the reported exposure
HSV PCR from a fresh vesicle or ulcer base confirms the diagnosis; type-specific IgG distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2
HIV and syphilis testing are offered with any new genital ulcer because look-alikes must be excluded
Red flags such as fever with headache, confusion, seizure or focal deficit raise concern for herpes encephalitis and prompt empiric IV acyclovir

easy: Young adult with recurrent grouped painful vesicles on the lip or genitals
Clear tingling prodrome before the eruption
Tender regional lymphadenopathy and no systemic illness
medium: Primary genital episode with fever, dysuria and severe pain but no prior history
Orolabial lesions in a child with fever and refusal to eat (gingivostomatitis)
Immunocompromised patient with more extensive or slowly healing lesions
Patient with a single ulcer where syphilis must also be considered
hard: Atypical orofacial pain or neuralgia without obvious vesicles, especially in an older adult
Genital ulcer in pregnancy near delivery, where neonatal transmission risk changes management
Lesions in an unusual site such as a finger (herpetic whitlow) or the eye
Fever with headache, confusion or seizure suggesting herpes encephalitis rather than isolated skin disease
Coexisting look-alike such as syphilis or chancroid with a negative or unavailable HSV swab
